title: The words you will hear every day
summary: Repository, working tree, branch, merge, pull request. Five words, each explained with the essay from the last lesson, so the rest of the course never has to stop and define them.

sections.heading: Repository: the folder plus its memory
sections.body:
A **repository** (everyone says **repo**) is an ordinary folder that Git is watching, together with the history of every commit ever made in it. On your computer it looks like any other folder. The history lives in a hidden sub-folder called `.git` that you never open by hand.

If you delete the `.git` folder, you have a normal folder again and the history is gone. If you copy the whole folder somewhere else, the history goes with it. Your essay folder becomes a repository the moment you run `git init` inside it.

sections.heading: Working tree: the files you can see right now
sections.body:
The **working tree** (also called the working directory) is simply the files in the folder as they are at this moment, the ones you open and edit. It is called a tree because a folder with sub-folders inside it branches out like a tree when you draw it.

The working tree can be different from the latest commit. You typed three new sentences into the essay since the last commit: the working tree has them, the history does not, until you commit. `git status` is how you ask "what is different between my working tree and my last commit?"

There is a third place in between, the staging area, where you choose what the next commit will contain. Track 02 has a whole lesson on it; for now just know that saving goes files → staging area → commit.

sections.heading: Branch: a separate line of saves
sections.body:
Imagine you want to try rewriting the ending of the essay, but you are not sure it will work out. You would rather not touch the good version. In Git you make a **branch**: a second line of commits that starts from where you are now and grows on its own.

The main line is called **main**. Your experiment lives on a branch called, say, `new-ending`. Commits you make while on `new-ending` do not change `main` at all. If the experiment fails, you throw the branch away and `main` is untouched. If it works, you bring it back in; that is the next word.

Branches are cheap: Git stores a branch as a tiny note saying "this line of saves currently ends at commit X". People make them many times a day. Switching between branches changes the files in your working tree to match that branch's latest commit.

sections.heading: Merge: bringing two lines back together
sections.body:
A **merge** takes the commits from one branch and combines them into another. You finished the new ending on `new-ending`; merging it into `main` makes `main` contain the new ending too. After that the branch has done its job and is usually deleted.

Most merges are automatic. Git looks at what changed on each side and combines them. If both sides changed the same lines of the same file, Git cannot know which version you want. It stops and asks you to decide. That pause is called a **merge conflict**. It is not an error; it is a question, and Track 03 teaches how to answer it calmly.

sections.heading: Pull request: asking for review before merging
sections.body:
On a team, you do not merge your own branch into `main` quietly. You open a **pull request** (some tools say merge request): a page on the hosting site that shows every change on your branch and says "please review this and, if it is good, merge it".

Teammates read the changes, leave comments, and either approve or ask for fixes. You push more commits to the same branch to address the comments. When it is approved, someone presses the merge button and your work lands on `main`.

The name is slightly odd: you are asking the maintainers to *pull* your branch in. The pull request is a feature of hosting sites like GitHub, not of Git itself; the next lessons explain that split.

sections.heading: The five words in one story
sections.body:
1. You make the essay folder a **repository**.
2. You edit the file; your **working tree** now differs from the last commit. You commit.
3. You want to try a new ending, so you create a **branch** and commit there.
4. It works, so you open a **pull request**; a friend reviews it.
5. It is approved and **merged** into main. The branch is deleted.

Every lab in this course is one of these steps, done for real.

takeaways: Repository = folder + its history. Working tree = the files as they are right now.
A branch is a separate line of commits; merging combines it back into another branch.
A pull request is a review step on the hosting site before a merge.

quiz.question: What is the working tree?
options: The files in the folder as they are right now, which may differ from the last commit
quiz.explanation: The working tree is what you see and edit. Commits are snapshots of it taken at moments you choose.

quiz.question: You commit while on a branch called new-ending. What happens to main?
options: Nothing; main is untouched until you merge
quiz.explanation: Each branch is its own line of commits. main only changes when something is merged into it.

quiz.question: What is a pull request?
options: A command that downloads the latest files
A request to review a branch and merge it into another
A way to delete a branch
quiz.explanation: A pull request is the review step on a hosting site. The merge happens when it is approved.
